passages.t: Cedar from Tyre, and a growing family
passages.happening: ‘Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, stonemasons, and carpenters, to build a palace for him’ (verse 1). ‘And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had highly exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel’ (verse 2). David takes more wives in Jerusalem and has more sons and daughters (verse 3), and their names are listed, Solomon among them (verses 4-7).
passages.hearers:
This short chapter sits between the two attempts to bring the ark to Jerusalem. In 2 Samuel 5 these same events come before the first attempt, so the Chronicler has moved them, to show during the three months of waiting that God had not turned against David.

Tyre, on the Phoenician coast north of Israel, was a wealthy trading city with access to the cedar forests of Lebanon, the prized building timber of the ancient world. A gift of materials and craftsmen from one king to another was diplomacy as much as generosity: it recognized the new king as a peer and opened trade. A palace of cedar was the visible sign that a ruler had arrived. A Hiram of Tyre also supplied Solomon for the temple; if he is the same king, his reign was long or this gift came late in David's reign. The Chronicler arranges by theme as much as by sequence, so the placement here does not settle the date.

David understood that his kingdom was exalted for the sake of God's people, not for his own. Many wives were a mark of royal status and alliance in that world, though the law for kings warned against it, and the later story of David's sons shows the cost.
passages.later: A psalm of Solomon says, ‘Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain’ (Psalm 127:1).
passages.asks: David saw that his kingdom was raised up for the sake of God's people. Ask for whose sake you have been given what you have. And ask what success might tempt you to treat it as your own.

passages.t: Two battles, and a sound in the treetops
passages.happening:
When the Philistines hear that David has been anointed king over all Israel, they come looking for him and raid the Valley of Rephaim (verses 8-9). So David inquires of God, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” (verse 10). The LORD tells him to go, and David defeats them at Baal-perazim, saying, “Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand” (verse 11). The Philistines leave their gods behind, ‘and David ordered that they be burned in the fire’ (verse 12).

The Philistines raid again, and again David asks God (verses 13-14). This time God says not to march straight up but to circle round, and ‘As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle, because this will mean that God has marched out before you’ (verse 15). David does as God commanded and strikes the Philistines from Gibeon to Gezer (verse 16). ‘And David’s fame went out into every land, and the LORD caused all nations to fear him’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The Philistines held the southern coastal plain in cities such as Gaza, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath and Ashkelon. While David was Saul's rival they had tolerated him. Once he was king over all Israel, he was a threat. The Valley of Rephaim lies just south-west of Jerusalem, so the attack came close to the new capital.

The two battles follow the same pattern: a raid, David asks God, God answers, David obeys, and victory follows. The repetition is the point. David does not assume that the first answer covers the second situation. He asks again, and receives a different plan. Saul's name means asked for, and Saul did not ask; David does.

Armies carried images of their gods into battle as a pledge of help, so leaving them behind meant total rout. Second Samuel says that David and his men carried the idols away; the Chronicler adds that David had them burned, as the law required. The place name Baal-perazim, lord of breaking through, echoes chapter 13: there the LORD broke out against Uzzah, and here he breaks out against Israel's enemies. The same holy power that endangers careless worship protects an obedient people. The kind of tree in verse 14 is uncertain.
passages.later: Second Samuel says that ‘David and his men carried them away’ (2 Samuel 5:21). The law had said of other gods' images, ‘burn their idols in the fire’ (Deuteronomy 7:5).
passages.asks: David asked God before the second battle, even though he had won the first. Ask where you have assumed that what worked before will work again. And ask when you last waited for God to move before you did.
